structure.title: Naming good and evil
structure.text: The first essay proposes an account of how opposing moral vocabularies arise from different positions of power.

structure.title: Guilt and self-denial
structure.text: The second and third essays investigate conscience, punishment, and ascetic ideals, extending the inquiry into the uses of suffering.

people.name: Ressentiment
people.text: A persistent hostility that helps create values.

context.title: Genealogy
context.text: Nietzsche asks how values developed and what needs they serve. His historical stories and his assessments of value need separate examination.
context.takeaway: An origin story does not settle present worth.

context.title: Polemic
context.text: The book addresses opponents aggressively and gives hypotheses dramatic force. Its confidence is a rhetorical feature, not independent evidence.

notice.why: Words can preserve a struggle after its circumstances change.
The need for meaning helps sustain costly ideals.

opening: A person who cannot strike back can still declare the enemy evil and make helplessness sound virtuous. Nietzsche asks how much of our moral language may have developed through transformations like that. He digs beneath guilt, punishment, and self-denial, looking for the desires that respectable explanations conceal. His history is deliberately provocative, and its claims need resisting as well as following. The disturbance comes from seeing qualities we praise acquire an ancestry that their admirers would rather leave out of the family story.
